name: WasmNow
baseline: V8 Liftoff (Chrome's WebAssembly baseline compiler); Wasmer Singlepass
workload: Single-pass baseline compilation of WebAssembly with the copy-and-patch technique, measured as compile time and generated-code speed on the Coremark and PolyBenchC suites.
claimed_speedup: Coremark: 'we compile 5x faster while also generating 39% faster code' than Liftoff; PolyBenchC: 'we compile 6.5x faster while also generating 63% faster code'. README also says it beats Wasmer Singlepass in both compile speed and code quality, without giving numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Built with the repo's own 'pochivm-build ... production' script inside docker; exact compiler version and flags not stated in the README.
tradeoffs: WebAssembly 1.0 core only, partial WASI, Linux-only docker build, and the author says the code is rushed with large amounts of dead code. A baseline compiler: the faster code is relative to Liftoff, not to optimizing tiers such as V8 TurboFan or Cranelift. Security warning in README: do not run untrusted modules.
caveats: The OOPSLA 2021 paper (Copy-and-Patch Compilation, Distinguished Paper Award) carries the full methodology including the CPU, but arXiv, the author's site and sillycross.github.io were blocked, so the paper was not opened; the numbers come from the README (which matches the figures the search snippet quoted from the abstract). Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper plus public benchmark code; CPU model and flags were not verified. Repo is a proof of concept, last commit 2021, author says no plan to continue. Benchmark code is in the repo as gtest cases (WasmCompilation.BenchmarkAll).
found_via: WebSearch: copy-and-patch OR "template JIT" WebAssembly compiler paper open source "faster than" Liftoff OR Winch OR "wasm3" compile time github

name: WAVM
baseline: Wasmer (LLVM backend), Wasmtime, V8 (Node.js), Lucet, Wasmer Singlepass
workload: libsodium 1.0.18 built-in cryptographic benchmark suite compiled to WASI, run on each WebAssembly runtime (Intel CPU machines on macOS, with a Linux x86_64 run for the LLVM-based runtimes).
claimed_speedup: 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test'; 'WAVM was still about 15% faster than wasmer' (LLVM backend); V8 (Node.js) second, then Wasmer Singlepass, Wasmtime, Lucet slowest. No per-test numbers in the README text (results are charts).
compiler_and_flags: All runtimes compiled from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js from stock binaries); libsodium 1.0.18-stable built with system LLVM 11.1.0 via Homebrew, same default optimization flags for native and WebAssembly builds.
hardware: Intel CPU machines (macOS) plus a Linux/x86_64 machine; CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: LLVM ahead-of-time/JIT compile: high compile latency and large LLVM dependency, so a poor fit for cold-start-bound workloads. Supports WebAssembly 1.0 plus several proposals (WASI, SIMD, threads, reference types).
caveats: Independent shootout, but data are from February 2021 and the repo's result charts are images; WAVM was not run on ARM. The newer 2022-12 results folder holds only images and raw data and the 2023/2026 posts on 00f.net are blocked; a search snippet for the 2026 post says wasmer is the best performer with WAVM, WAMR and Wasmtime close, so the ranking may have changed. WAVM's last commit is recent (2026-04-04) but its pace is slow.
found_via: Page https://github.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks (libsodium WebAssembly benchmarks) reached from WebSearch 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer' and github.com topics/webassembly-runtime; WAVM README opened for metadata

name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter; wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: 39-case interpreter harness (17 cases that every runtime runs): fib, sieve, crc32, call_indirect, vtable dispatch, xmrsplayer tracker player, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP; CPU time per call at N=10 on E-cores of an M4 Max and an iPhone XS Max, JIT/AOT disabled in all runtimes.
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geomean over 17 cases: wasm3 1.01, wamr 1.63, wasmtime Pulley 2.09, wasmz 1.59, tinywasm 3.20, WasmEdge 8.42 on M4 Max E-cores (about 1.6x faster than WAMR and 2.1x faster than Pulley, derived from page data); iPhone XS: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68. call_indirect: wasm3 11.67 ms vs WAMR 18.48 ms vs Pulley 31.53 ms per call (M4). The 2021 libsodium shootout also says WAMR 'was slower than wasm3 on every single test'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions on Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27); WAMR main b70d708d with cmake Release -O3 and AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off; Pulley from wasmtime v49 fork with --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO.
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (macOS 27.0) and iPhone XS Max (A12 Bionic) E-cores
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with a small footprint (about 64 KB code, 10 KB RAM per README); it cannot run SIMD, exceptions, GC, typed references, memory64 or multi-memory, so it ran only about 22 of the 39 harness cases. README says the repo is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Result is interpreter versus interpreter: wasm3's own docs/Performance.md (2019-2020, i5-8250U, CoreMark) shows wasmtime 4.0x and Wasmer Cranelift 4.0x faster than wasm3, and WAMR 8.1x slower, so JIT runtimes still win on sustained compute. In the 2026 harness wasm3's instantiate cost on extended-const modules is 116-122x Pulley's. The harness author maintains a wasmtime fork and applies 29 patches to WAMR and 26 to WasmEdge, but none to wasm3 (v0.9.0 unpatched). The Pulley row is wasmtime's interpreter backend, not its native JIT.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' (site filter github.com) surfaced rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark and wasm3 docs/Performance.md

name: WAMR (WebAssembly Micro Runtime) fast interpreter
workload: Same 39-case interpreter harness as the wasm3 entry (17 cases common to all runtimes): CPU time per call on M4 Max and iPhone XS Max E-cores with JIT/AOT disabled.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to fastest: WAMR 1.63 vs Pulley 2.09 on M4 Max E-cores (about 1.28x faster, derived from page data) and 1.38 vs 1.68 on iPhone XS (about 1.22x, derived). Per case on M4: bulk_memory 10.41 vs 22.14 ms, call_indirect 18.48 vs 31.53 ms, convolution 3.928 vs 5.883 ms, sieve 0.5128 vs 0.7082 ms. Separately, the repo's own cross-runtime doc says WAMR is 1.37-1.86x faster than Pulley on iPhone 12 across call_indirect, xmrsplayer, vtable and graphql (AssemblyScript).
compiler_and_flags: cmake Release, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 etc., WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1, Apple clang 21.0.0; 29 local patches applied to WAMR main b70d708d (2026-09-21).
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (macOS 27.0) and iPhone XS Max (A12 Bionic)
tradeoffs: Fast-interpreter mode only in this comparison (AOT and JIT disabled by the App-Store constraint). Footprint about 58.9K for the fast interpreter per README. The measured build lacks GC, typed references, memory64, multi-memory and exnref.
caveats: The win is interpreter versus wasmtime's Pulley interpreter, not versus wasmtime's native Cranelift JIT, which is far faster than both. WAMR is also slower than wasm3 in the same harness (1.63 vs 1.01 geomean) and than wasm3 in the 2021 libsodium shootout, and the wasmz benchmark shows it behind wasmz and wasm3. The Pulley build carries the harness author's own optimization patches (9 commits), so Pulley is if anything flattered. WAMR itself is also a baseline named for this category, so treat as a relative claim.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' (site filter github.com) surfaced rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark

name: wasmz
workload: Interpreter run time of fib(30) compiled from C, QuickJS fib(25) inside WASM (1.4 MB module) and esbuild bundling inside WASM (19 MB module), median of 20 runs after 5 warmups.
claimed_speedup: fib(30): wasmz 37.0 ms vs wasmi 38.4, wasm3 39.7, WAMR 49.6. QuickJS fib(25): 174.9 ms vs wasmi 184.4, wasm3 217.4, WAMR 242.9. esbuild: 909.5 ms vs wasmi 918.2, wasm3 2215.0 (WAMR excluded, it overflowed the stack). README: 'currently the fastest WebAssembly interpreter I have tested'.
compiler_and_flags: wasmz dev ReleaseFast (Zig); other runtimes' build flags not stated.
hardware: Linux 6.17.0-1010-azure x86_64 (Azure VM), CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Register-IR plus direct-threaded interpreter with accumulator registers and superinstructions; supports GC, SIMD, exceptions, threading, WASI preview 1; C and Zig APIs. Peak RSS on fib(30) 17.3 MB vs WAMR 11.0 MB.
caveats: First-party numbers, CPU not stated, and the wasm3 used is old v0.5.1 (current v0.9.0). The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (M4 Max, 2026-09-22) ranks wasmz behind wasm3 (geomean 1.59 vs 1.01), roughly level with WAMR (1.63) and ahead of wasmtime Pulley (2.09), and reports that wasmz fails six rows (2 wrong results, 2 traps, 2 crashes) and never collects GC structs. Treat the win over WAMR as unconfirmed.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' -> rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark comparison table, then github.com/Ray-D-Song/wasmz

name: zwasm
workload: End-to-end wall time of '<runtime> run <module>' (spawn, instantiate, execute WASI _start) with hyperfine on short TinyGo and ClojureWasm guests, plus peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
claimed_speedup: Startup-bound short workloads (mean ms): tinygo/fib zwasm-aot 2.0, interp 2.3, jit 2.8 vs wasmtime 7.2, wazero 7.1, wasmer 12.0, WasmEdge 16.5. Peak RSS on tinygo/fib: zwasm-aot 2.1 MB, jit 3.2, interp 2.7 vs wazero 8.7, wasmtime 13.3, WasmEdge 23.7, wasmer 27.5 ('4-12x less').
compiler_and_flags: zwasm built ReleaseFast (Zig); comparators pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench; hyperfine 5 runs plus 3 warmup.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (Mac aarch64), one host
tradeoffs: Single-pass JIT, interpreter and AOT backends with Wasm 3.0 and WASI 0.2/0.3; small footprint and fast startup traded for peak throughput.
caveats: The doc is explicit that the optimizing JITs lead on sustained compute: wasmtime/wasmer/wazero beat zwasm-jit/aot by about 1.5-3.9x (shootout/fib2 zwasm-jit 1077 ms vs wasmtime 700 ms; base64 about 13.7x slower). The startup rows are dominated by process start, not execution. The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark found zwasm's interpreter about 8.5x slower than the fastest interpreter (geomean 8.47 vs wasm3 1.01). A fork's README (andypeng2015/zwasm) says the 'majority match or beat wasmtime' on 29 benchmarks, which the canonical benchmarks doc does not support. github.com/clojurewasm/zwasm served the same content (186 stars) and its links point into zwasm/zwasm, so the repo appears to have moved or been renamed.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' (zwasm result), then docs/benchmarks.md fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com/clojurewasm/zwasm

name: aWsm
baseline: Wasmer; WAVM; Lucet; Node.js with Emscripten; wasm3 on microcontrollers
workload: PolyBench/C slowdown over native C, on x86-64, aarch64 (Raspberry Pi) and Cortex-M4/M7, for an ahead-of-time Wasm-to-LLVM compiler with a small C runtime.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 average slowdown over native: Wasmer 149.8%, WAVM 28.1%, Node.js + Emscripten 84.0%, Lucet 92.8%, aWsm 13.4%. aarch64: aWsm 6.7%. Cortex-M7 40.2% and M4 24.9%, versus 'more than 10x' for the wasm3 interpreter on microcontrollers (links wasm3's Performance.md).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler through LLVM, so compile latency; the runtime is under 5K lines of C and the compiler under 3.5K lines of Rust; output is ELF objects; seven selectable memory-bounds-check mechanisms. Not a fit where interpreters or JIT are required.
caveats: README states 'these numbers are from May 2020'; hardware, compiler versions and flags are not given in the README (EMSOFT 2020 paper and Sledge Middleware 2020 paper hold the details, but www2.seas.gwu.edu was blocked). Wasmtime is not in the x86-64 table (the table shows Wasmer, WAVM, Node.js+Emscripten, Lucet); Wasmer and Lucet versions are 2020-era. Rust compiler plus C runtime, so only the generated objects and runtime are callable from C++. Repo remains active (last commit 2026-07-13).
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly AOT OR JIT compiler paper artifact github evaluation wasmtime WAMR wasmer speedup single-pass baseline compiler' surfaced gwsystems/aWsm

name: LFI (Lightweight Fault Isolation)
baseline: LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly compilers (not named in README; Wasmtime, Wasmer and wasm2c are the usual ones)
workload: Run-time overhead versus native code on the SPEC 2017 benchmark suite (compatible subset) for in-process software sandboxing of native Arm64 and x86-64 code, compared with the overhead WebAssembly sandboxing imposes.
claimed_speedup: LFI: 7% runtime overhead (Arm64) or 8% (x86-64) for full read and write isolation, 1.5% (Arm64) or 6% (x86-64) for writes only, versus 'LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly compilers, which incur upwards of 20% runtime overhead' (lfi-research branch README).
compiler_and_flags: LFI-patched LLVM toolchain (lfi-llvm-toolchain); flags not stated in README.
tradeoffs: Sandboxes native C/C++/assembly rather than Wasm bytecode: no stable binary format, no platform independence, Arm64 and x86-64 only (RISC-V experimental); needs an LFI compiler toolchain and a verifier; ~64K (Arm64) or ~3K (x86-64) sandboxes of up to 4 GiB per address space.
caveats: The Wasm comparison figure is a summary line in the README; the per-runtime numbers sit in the ASPLOS 2024 paper (Yedidia, Lightweight Fault Isolation), which was not opened (scs.stanford.edu and zyedidia.github.io blocked). The baseline is not named in the README, so the exact WebAssembly runtime is unconfirmed (confidence capped at 0.5). A search snippet quoting a different source gives Wasmtime about 150% and wasm2c about 197% of native run time; not verified here. Different execution model from a Wasm VM: it replaces Wasm rather than running it faster.
found_via: WebSearch: 'software fault isolation sandbox faster than WebAssembly wasm2c Wasmtime WAMR overhead paper LFI OR Segue github'

name: WAMR in Zig (cataggar/wamr)
workload: Cold start of a 36-byte no-op module (subprocess wall time, 20 samples after 3 warmups) comparing in-process JIT, AOT cold and warm modes against 'wasmtime run', plus CoreMark steady state.
claimed_speedup: Cold start median: in-process JIT (.fast preset) 1.430 ms vs wasmtime 6.964 ms (about 4.9x faster); AOT warm 1.182 ms; AOT cold 2.552 ms. CoreMark steady state: wasmtime 26,462.6 iter/s vs JIT .fast 12,002.8 and AOT 12,442.8, i.e. wasmtime about 2.1x faster.
compiler_and_flags: Zig build with -Djit=true -Doptimize=fast; scripts/bench_jit_coldstart.py; Zig version and wasmtime version not stated in the doc.
hardware: Azure VM, 8 vCPU, AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, x86_64
tradeoffs: Zig port of bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime kept as a separate fork (not drop-in for C++ callers without the Zig toolchain); passes the spec suite (257 .wast files, 65,135 assertions) per README; CLI is AOT/JIT only. Steady-state throughput is about half of wasmtime.
caveats: Cold-start win is on a trivial 36-byte module where wasmtime's fixed per-invocation cost dominates; the doc itself says wasmtime is about 2.1x faster on CoreMark. Single host, versions of wasmtime and Zig not stated, Small fork maintained with AI assistance (commit attribution and search snippet). Process spawn time is included in the numbers.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime paper faster than wasmtime V8 WAMR open source implementation github'

name: wisp
baseline: wasmtime Winch (baseline compiler); wasmer Singlepass; wasmtime Cranelift on fib
workload: Whole-process wall time (including startup and compilation) of seven programs (primes, fib, matmul, raytrace, compress, json, regex) compiled to wasm32-wasip1, plus compile-only time for a 1.36 MB regex.wasm; median of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: Compile-only regex.wasm: wisp 16 ms vs wasmtime Winch 24 ms, wasmer Singlepass 32 ms, wasmtime Cranelift 72 ms, wasmer Cranelift 82 ms. End to end: fib 34 wisp 0.022 s vs wasmtime Cranelift 0.024, Winch 0.031, wasmer Singlepass 0.028; raytrace 0.054 s vs Winch 0.066; json 0.263 s vs Winch 0.325; regex 0.308 s vs Winch 0.341 s.
compiler_and_flags: Release builds; wasmtime 49.0.1 and wasmer 7.5.0 release binaries; bench/run.py method documented in README.
tradeoffs: Compact (about 12,600 lines of Rust) runtime with validator, register-style interpreter and a single-pass AArch64 baseline compiler (macOS AArch64 only, Linux paths untested); passes 27,416 spec assertions on both engines; explicit bounds checks and no cross-block register allocation.
caveats: README states plainly that it is 1.5-2.5x slower than wasmtime Cranelift end to end on six of seven programs, loses to Winch on primes, compress and matmul, and wasmtime/wasmer compile in parallel and write artefacts while wisp compiles single-threaded, so the compile-time comparison is not like for like. Own benchmarks only, 0 stars, 15 commits when viewed, very new. Rust and AArch64-only compiler, not callable from C++ without bindings.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Whose baseline compiler is it anyway Wizard single-pass compiler Liftoff Winch Wasmer compile speed results' surfaced useless-husband/wisp

name: Silverfir-nano
baseline: wasmtime Cranelift 47.0.2; V8 TurboFan (Node.js 25.9); wasm3; wasmi 2.0.0-beta.7
workload: 15 WASI benchmark metrics (CoreMark, SHA-256, bzip2, LZ4, sqlite speedtest1, Lua scripts, mandelbrot, c-ray, STREAM) self-timed for 2 s on an Apple M4; JIT compared with optimizing compilers and interpreter compared with interpreters.
claimed_speedup: JIT at parity with Cranelift and V8: best-of-four over 15 metrics is Cranelift 9, Silverfir 4, V8 2; leads on SHA-256 250.6 vs Cranelift 216.8 MB/s (+16%) and bzip2 30.68 vs 26.86 MB/s (+14%); CoreMark 44,958 vs Cranelift 45,874 vs V8 44,378; beats V8 on mandelbrot 1.68x. Interpreter: CoreMark 8,586.4 vs wasm3 4,268 and wasmi 5,482; wins 14 of 15 metrics by 1.16-2.01x over wasm3 and 1.07-2.41x over wasmi (margin over the faster rival 1.07-1.69x, median about 1.39x).
compiler_and_flags: Silverfir built --release; wasmtime/Cranelift 47.0.2 built from source with rustc 1.97.0; wasm3 build-release; benchmark wasm regenerated with current wasi-sdk clang; run_tests.py and run_v8.mjs are in the repo.
tradeoffs: no_std runtime with both a JIT and an interpreter on six ISAs (x86_64, ARM64, RISC-V, Thumb-2); flash 337 KiB interpreter and 1,042 KiB JIT on RP2350; Wasm 3.0 features but the interpreter excludes SIMD and GC; Rust, so C++ embedding needs bindings.
caveats: First-party suite, one machine (M4), interpreters are single runs while compiled engines are the mean of two rounds; Cranelift still wins 9 of 15 metrics and is ahead on sqlite and LZ4 decompress (3,478 vs 3,241), so the claim is parity, not a win. Wasmtime 47.0.2 and V8 14.1 are older than current releases, the file states the numbers are dated 2026-07-24 and share no baseline with earlier revisions, and CoreMark runs in a non-standard bounded regression mode. Silverfir also appears among 23 engines in the wasmi-benchmarks suite (results only as plots, not read).
found_via: github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks README runtime list (reached via tinywasm README), then mbbill/Silverfir-nano README and benchmarks/wasi/RESULTS.md

name: Stitch
workload: CoreMark score of the WebAssembly build on Apple M2 Pro, Intel Xeon E312xx and Intel i9-13900K, compared across Stitch, Wasm3, Wasmi and Wasmtime.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark Mac/Linux/Windows: Stitch 2950 / 1684 / 4592, Wasm3 2911 / 1734 / 3951, Wasmi 788 / 645 / 1574, Wasmtime 12807 / 13724 / 34796. README: slightly faster than Wasm3 on Mac, slightly slower on Linux, significantly faster on Windows (derived from page data: about 1.16x on Windows).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README beyond running the coremark directory.
hardware: Apple M2 Pro 3.5 GHz; Intel Xeon E312xx 2.1 GHz; Intel i9-13900K 3.0 GHz
tradeoffs: Threaded-code interpreter that relies on LLVM sibling-call optimization (not guaranteed); 64-bit only, no SIMD, no WASI; about 15,000 lines with zero non-dev dependencies.
caveats: Only a single CoreMark workload; the edge over wasm3 is within a few percent on Mac and negative on Linux, and Wasmtime's JIT is 4-8x faster than Stitch, so it does not beat any JIT baseline in the category. Wasm3 and Wasmi versions are not stated. In the independent 2026 harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark, wasm3 is fastest interpreter on most cases (Stitch was not included there).
found_via: github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks README runtime list ('Experimental and very fast zero-dependencies Wasm interpreter'), then makepad/stitch README
